editorialRead.readHeadline: mastra-ai/mastra is the first source to inspect.
editorialRead.oneLineSummary: mastra-ai/mastra leads a 3-item attention queue backed by direct receipts; 27 watchlist sources are fresh, 0 need source-health attention, and movement still requires editorial judgment.
editorialRead.dek: Agent Pulse filtered 27 included projects down to 3 items worth finite newsroom attention. The queue protects attention; it does not declare winners.
bullets: mastra-ai/mastra — 1 commit today and 1 same-day mapped article, 39.6 below its current daily pace, with 3 hardening-subject points. Inspect the receipt before assigning a story.
openclaw/openclaw — 37 commits landed today. Keep it on watch, but require the next receipt to prove a reader consequence before promoting it.
browser-use/browser-use — No same-day commit after 22 commits in the seven-day window. The pause is notable enough to preserve, not enough to turn into a story.
editorialRead.watchNext: The next meaningful upgrade is feedback flow: issues opened and closed, review latency, stale backlog, and the share of work that starts outside the maintainer team.
editorialRead.caveat: Source-code motion and article coverage are collected. GitHub issue flow, PR review timing, community discussion, and private backlog signals are not.

dailyInsight.headline: Watch whether a repository cleanup hook survives the real retirement path
dailyInsight.insight: Mastra Factory has added a repository-specific teardown command to agent-session retirement, but the public evidence is still main-branch code and focused tests. Builders who run reusable agent workspaces should not promote this into a production cleanup dependency yet. Watch for a release or integration receipt that exercises a configured hook through a real sandbox interruption, then verify that generic scrub, binding removal, and the next repository claim still occur in the promised order.
dailyInsight.mechanism: The new Factory retirement coordinator serializes cleanup for each session, attempts the linked repository's teardown command before remote release or local destruction, and then continues with scrub, pooling or destruction, cache invalidation, and optional session deletion. Its tests require the hook to run before scrub/pooling/invalidation, continue cleanup after a failing hook, and avoid duplicate teardown under concurrent retirement requests.
dailyInsight.whyItMatters: A generic reset cannot know every project-specific service, generated artifact, or checkout convention. But a project hook is not an integrity proof either: it can fail, hang, or be incomplete. The useful operational question is whether the platform preserves its independent recovery invariants after that hook reports trouble, rather than whether a cleanup script exists.

actions.audience: Builder or operator evaluating reusable coding-agent sandboxes or worktrees
actions.label: Track a real lifecycle receipt before depending on the hook
actions.instruction: Keep any current cleanup path unchanged. Watch Mastra's release and integration evidence for a configured teardown run through a disposable repository and a provider interruption. When such a path is public, reproduce it only in a non-production workspace with a harmless marker-file hook, then verify the hook order, generic scrub or destruction, cleared session binding, and clean next claim. Do not use a teardown command that deletes broad filesystem paths or production credentials.
actions.effort: 10 minutes to track; 30–60 minutes for a disposable verification once a released path is available

receipts.title: feat(factory): add per-repository worktree teardown commands (#21564)
receipts.supports: Shows the public implementation change adding per-repository teardown commands to Factory cleanup and its coding-agent co-author attribution.

receipts.title: Factory session retirement tests at commit #21564
receipts.supports: Shows source-level checks for teardown ordering, continued cleanup after failure, local destruction ordering, missing-sandbox handling, and serialized duplicate retirement.

confidence.basis: One fresh public project change and its focused tests agree on a narrow lifecycle contract. The call is to watch and verify a future released or integrated path, not to claim provider reliability, deployment availability, or full cleanup assurance.

dailyInsight.limitation: The receipts are main-branch implementation and tests. They do not prove the feature is released, that any project has a safe or complete teardown command, that arbitrary hooks are isolated, or that cleanup succeeds across every sandbox provider and interruption mode.
dailyInsight.falsifier: Revise this call if public integration evidence shows the configured hook can run after generic scrub or after a workspace has been returned to the pool, can run twice for one session binding, or can prevent the platform from clearing the binding and recovering the resource without a documented operator decision.
dailyInsight.watchNext: Watch for a release note, public provider integration test, or operator report that follows a configured teardown through failure, provider reattachment, scrub or destruction, and the next repository claim.
